messages.subject: Variance Estimation for Point Counts
parts:
Hello,

I have a couple of questions regarding variance estimations for point count surveys.

First, our point locations are not randomly distributed throughout our study area, but rather are in a systematic random grid. I believe that the basic settings within Distance are set to calculate variances based on random placement of points, and that it is overestimating the variance if points are systematic randomly placed. How do you correct for this in Distance? I know for line transects you can select the advanced option of post-stratifying samples (I believe it is selecting the bottom radio button in the advanced option of the variance tab). Is it the same for point transects?

Second, is bootstrapping variance estimates always considered a good idea or are the specific scenarios where it is not necessary or conversely, extremely necessary?

I appreciate any input regarding these topics.

Best,

John Edwards
Ph.D. Research Assistant
Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute
Texas A&M University - Kingsville
405-246-6540

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: Variance Estimation for Point Counts
parts:
Hi John

The post-stratification method, described by Fewster et al. (2009) can be applied to points, as demonstrated in the handout material from the precision lecture in the introductory workshop notes. However, because points are of "equal length", they are less likely to suffer from the extreme encounter rate heterogeneity that comes from high animal density occurring on short lines and low animal density on long lines; hence post-stratification is less likely to have much consequence.

My personal opinion is that bootstrapping is always a good idea, because computing power is sufficient such that it takes little effort on the users' part. Bootstrapping reduces the number of assumptions and approximations employed in producing your estimates of precision. There is little cost to performing the bootstrap calculations.
